title: When the contract ends badly
subtitle: Wrongful dismissal, notice and damages at common law
objectives: Distinguish wrongful dismissal, a breach-of-contract claim, from unfair dismissal, a statutory claim — and explain why the two protect different interests
State how damages for wrongful dismissal are calculated by reference to the contractual notice period, and identify what the claim cannot compensate
Apply the wrongful dismissal analysis to a fact pattern, correctly classifying notice, pay in lieu, garden leave and repudiatory breach by either party

leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms damages for wrongful dismissal cannot extend to the manner of dismissal or injury to feelings — the 'Johnson exclusion zone'

leadingAuthorities.citation: Malik v Bank of Credit and Commerce International SA [1997] UKHL 23
leadingAuthorities.role: Recognises stigma damages for breach of the implied term of trust and confidence occurring during employment, as distinct from the dismissal itself

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: The single most common exam error in this area is answering a wrongful dismissal problem as though it were an unfair dismissal problem — reaching for 'was this reasonable?' when the only question is 'what does the contract say, and was it honoured?'. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the notice rules — this lesson is about not reaching for the wrong claim.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below is weighted towards scenarios that mix wrongful and unfair dismissal facts together: expect to have to say which claim is even available.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about the difference between a contract claim and a statutory claim before moving on — every later part in this lesson assumes you can keep the two apart.

overview.hook: An employee is marched out of the building without a word of explanation, told to collect her belongings by security. It feels like the worst kind of dismissal — and it might be. But if her employer paid her three months' salary in lieu of the three months' notice her contract required, she may have no wrongful dismissal claim at all. The law of wrongful dismissal doesn't ask whether the employer behaved decently. It asks one narrower question: did the contract get performed?

parts.heading: Two claims that sound alike and are not
parts.voice: structural — draws the boundary the rest of the lesson depends on
body: Students arrive at this topic already primed to think about dismissal in terms of fairness, because 'unfair dismissal' is the phrase that dominates popular understanding of employment law. Wrongful dismissal asks a completely different question, and it predates the statutory scheme by centuries: it is an ordinary breach of contract claim, brought at common law, and it succeeds or fails entirely on the terms of the contract of employment.

A dismissal is 'wrongful' when the employer terminates the contract in a way that itself breaches its terms — most commonly, by dismissing the employee with no notice, or with less notice than the contract (or the statutory minimum) requires, and without paying in lieu. Note what is irrelevant to this claim: whether the employer had a good reason to dismiss, whether the process was fair, how long the employee had worked there, and how the dismissal was communicated. None of that features. The only question is contractual performance.

This means wrongful dismissal is available from day one of employment — there is no qualifying period, because it isn't a statutory right at all. It also means a wrongful dismissal claim can, in principle, sit alongside a completely fair unfair dismissal outcome, or a completely unfair one: the two claims run on independent tracks and ask independent questions.

components.definition: A common law breach of contract claim arising where an employer terminates the contract of employment other than in accordance with its terms — typically by dismissing without the notice, or payment in lieu of notice, the contract requires. It is distinct from, and does not depend on, the statutory unfair dismissal scheme.

interaction.prompt: An employee with four months' service is dismissed with no notice and no payment in lieu, in breach of her contract. Can she bring a wrongful dismissal claim despite having under two years' service?
options: Yes — wrongful dismissal has no qualifying period, because it is a contract claim, not a statutory one
No — the same two-year qualifying period that applies to unfair dismissal applies here too
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The qualifying period is a feature of the statutory unfair dismissal scheme; a breach of contract claim needs nothing more than a contract that was breached.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what kind of claim this is. Wrongful dismissal is ordinary contract law — qualifying periods belong to the statutory scheme covered in the next two lessons, and simply don't apply here.

parts.heading: Notice, pay in lieu, and garden leave
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Every contract of employment carries a notice entitlement, set by whichever is longer of the contractual notice period and the statutory minimum in s 86 ERA 1996. The statutory minimum rises with length of service and functions as a floor the contract cannot go beneath, however short the contractual notice clause tries to make it.

An employer who wants to end the relationship immediately, without requiring the employee to work out their notice, has two lawful routes. The first is payment in lieu of notice (a 'PILON'): if the contract contains a PILON clause, the employer can dismiss on the spot and pay a sum equal to the salary (and often benefits) the employee would have earned during the notice period — this is a contractual mechanism for ending the relationship early, not a breach. The second is garden leave: the employee remains formally employed and paid throughout the notice period, bound by all contractual duties including fidelity and confidentiality, but is instructed not to attend work or perform duties. Garden leave keeps the contract alive; a PILON (properly exercised) ends it.

The trap is an employer who does neither properly — who simply stops paying and stops requiring attendance, with no PILON clause authorising that step. That is not garden leave and not a valid PILON. It is a failure to give notice, and it is a breach: wrongful dismissal, in its plainest form.

components.text: The notice required to be given by an employer to terminate the contract of employment of a person who has been continuously employed for one month or more — (a) is not less than one week's notice if his period of continuous employment is less than two years, (b) is not less than one week's notice for each year of continuous employment if his period of continuous employment is two years or more but less than twelve years, and (c) is not less than twelve weeks' notice if his period of continuous employment is twelve years or more.
elements: One week's notice under two years' service
One week per completed year of service, from two up to twelve years
A twelve-week statutory ceiling once service reaches twelve years
Operates as a floor beneath the contractual notice period, not a substitute for it

interaction.prompt: Put these in the order a properly exercised PILON clause operates.
items: The contract of employment contains an express PILON clause
The employer decides to end the relationship immediately rather than have the employee work notice
The employer pays a sum equivalent to salary (and contractual benefits) for the notice period
The contract terminates immediately, lawfully, with no breach
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the mechanism: the PILON clause is what makes immediate termination-plus-payment lawful. Without step 1, steps 2–4 collapse into an ordinary breach.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The clause has to come first — a PILON only works because the contract itself authorises it. Paying money on dismissal without that clause doesn't automatically cure a failure to give notice.

parts.heading: Repudiatory breach cuts both ways
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the doctrine through Malik before naming it
body: Wrongful dismissal is usually framed as something an employer does to an employee, but the underlying doctrine is symmetrical: a repudiatory breach — a breach going to the root of the contract — entitles the innocent party to treat the contract as at an end, whichever side commits it.

On the employee's side, this is why gross misconduct justifies summary dismissal without notice: theft, violence, or a serious breach of the duty of fidelity are treated as the employee's own repudiatory breach, releasing the employer from the obligation to give notice at all. On the employer's side, the same principle underpins constructive dismissal — an employer's repudiatory breach entitles the employee to resign and treat themselves as dismissed.

Malik v BCCI shows how wide the employer's obligations run. BCCI collapsed amid findings of pervasive fraud. Employees who had done nothing wrong found themselves unemployable afterwards, tainted by association with a bank later shown to have been run corruptly — even though their own dismissals were procedurally unremarkable. The House of Lords held that operating a business in a corrupt and dishonest manner breached the implied term of mutual trust and confidence owed to every employee, and that 'stigma damages' for the resulting loss of employability were recoverable — not because of how the employees were dismissed, but because of what the employer had done to the relationship during the employment itself.

components.caseName: Malik v Bank of Credit and Commerce International SA
components.factsShort: BCCI collapsed after being run in a corrupt and dishonest manner. Former employees, innocent of wrongdoing, found the stigma of having worked there made them unemployable in banking.
components.ratioShort: Operating a business dishonestly and corruptly breaches the implied term of trust and confidence owed to employees; resulting 'stigma' loss to employability is recoverable in damages.

expanded.facts: BCCI's liquidators sought recovery, but former employees counterclaimed for damages, arguing that the bank's corrupt manner of operation — later exposed in detail — had damaged their reputations in the banking sector and made them unable to find comparable work, even though none of them had personally been dismissed unfairly or accused of wrongdoing.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The House of Lords held that the implied term of mutual trust and confidence is broken not only by conduct directed at the employee personally, but by an employer conducting its business in a manner calculated or likely to destroy or seriously damage the relationship of trust and confidence, judged objectively. Damages for the resulting handicap in the labour market — 'stigma damages' — were in principle recoverable as ordinary contractual loss.
expanded.significance: Malik confirms that wrongful dismissal thinking is not limited to the dismissal event itself: breaches of the trust and confidence term occurring during employment are actionable in contract, and can produce loss (like stigma) that is different in kind from lost notice pay. It sits alongside Johnson v Unisys as the doctrinal pairing that defines the outer edge of what contract damages in the employment context can and cannot reach.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows the employee has committed a repudiatory breach entitling summary dismissal without notice.
interaction.scenarioText: Aiden is a warehouse supervisor. He has been slightly late twice this month. During a stock check, he is found to have been systematically falsifying delivery records to conceal stock he had been stealing over several months. His manager suspends him the same afternoon.
tappableSpans: systematically falsifying delivery records to conceal stock he had been stealing
interaction.correctSpan: systematically falsifying delivery records to conceal stock he had been stealing
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the repudiatory breach. Minor lateness is nowhere near serious enough to justify dismissal without notice; deliberate, sustained dishonesty and theft goes to the root of the employment relationship and entitles the employer to dismiss summarily.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for conduct serious enough to destroy the relationship outright, not routine timekeeping issues. Occasional lateness would never justify summary dismissal on its own; sustained theft and falsification of records is a different order of conduct entirely.

parts.heading: Johnson v Unisys: the exclusion zone
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the tempting argument before the House of Lords forecloses it
body: Here's an argument that feels obviously right and turns out to be wrong: if being dismissed in a brutal, humiliating way causes real psychiatric harm, surely a wrongful dismissal claim should compensate for that harm, on top of the lost notice pay?

Johnson v Unisys answers no. Mr Johnson was summarily dismissed following an internal disciplinary process that he argued was conducted unfairly and humiliatingly, and he suffered a psychiatric breakdown that, he said, permanently damaged his career. He sued in contract for damages going well beyond his notice pay, arguing the manner of his dismissal itself breached an implied term.

The House of Lords held that damages for wrongful dismissal are confined to the financial loss flowing from the failure to give proper notice — full stop. There is no recovery for injury to feelings, distress, or reputational harm caused by the manner of dismissal, however badly the employer behaved in carrying it out. Their Lordships reasoned that Parliament had already created a bespoke statutory scheme — unfair dismissal — precisely to police the manner and fairness of dismissals, complete with its own remedies and limits, and that expanding the common law claim to cover the same ground would circumvent the boundaries Parliament had deliberately drawn (including the qualifying period and statutory caps). This boundary is often called the 'Johnson exclusion zone'.

components.label: What wrongful dismissal damages cover — and don't
points: Covered: net pay and contractual benefits for the unexpired notice period, subject to the employee's duty to mitigate
Covered: other accrued contractual entitlements due but unpaid at termination (e.g. earned bonus, accrued holiday pay)
Not covered: injury to feelings or distress caused by how the dismissal was carried out (Johnson v Unisys)

Not covered: stigma or reputational loss caused by the dismissal event itself, as opposed to conduct during employment (contrast Malik, where the loss arose from the employer's conduct of the business, not the act of dismissal)
Not covered: loss of the chance to bring an unfair dismissal claim, or any enhancement reflecting how the employer behaved

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a wrongful dismissal claim can recover damages for psychiatric injury caused by a humiliating manner of dismissal?
interaction.explanation: Johnson v Unisys is unambiguous: damages for wrongful dismissal are confined to the financial loss from the notice period itself. Distress, injury to feelings and reputational harm caused by the manner of dismissal fall outside the claim entirely, however badly the employer behaved.

parts.heading: Calculating the loss
parts.voice: direct — works through the arithmetic examiners actually test
body: Once a breach is established, the damages calculation is a straightforward contract-law exercise: put the employee, so far as money can, in the position they would have been in had the contract been properly performed — which means paid, and working, through the full notice period.

That figure starts with net salary for the unexpired notice period, plus the value of contractual benefits that would have accrued over that period (pension contributions, health insurance, a company car's benefit value, and so on). But it is not simply handed over in full: the employee is under the ordinary contractual duty to mitigate their loss, meaning earnings from a new job found during what would have been the notice period are deducted from the award. If the contract entitled the employee to a discretionary bonus, whether that survives into the damages calculation depends on how the bonus scheme is drafted and whether the discretion was exercised in good faith.

Compare this tightly bounded, arithmetic exercise with the unfair dismissal compensatory award covered in later lessons — which considers the reasonableness of the dismissal, can include a basic award unrelated to notice, and is capped by statute rather than by the length of a notice clause. Keep the two calculations in separate mental boxes; conflating them is the single most common scoring error on this topic.

components.definition: A dismissed employee claiming wrongful dismissal damages must take reasonable steps to reduce their loss — typically by seeking alternative work. Earnings from a new job during what would have been the notice period are deducted from the damages award.

interaction.prompt: Two employees are dismissed with no notice, in clear breach of a six-month contractual notice clause. In which case is the wrongful dismissal damages award reduced by the duty to mitigate?
interaction.scenarioA: Employee A spends the six months searching for work but remains unemployed throughout, despite reasonable efforts.
interaction.scenarioB: Employee B finds an equivalent role paying the same salary after two months and works there for the remaining four months of what would have been her notice period.
interaction.explanation: B's damages for the final four months are reduced (potentially to nil for that period) because her new earnings offset the loss the notice-period claim exists to compensate. A, having mitigated reasonably but found nothing, recovers the full six months — mitigation only bites where it actually reduces loss.

testPool.prompt: Name the kind of legal claim wrongful dismissal is, and identify the one thing its damages compensate.
acceptableAnswers: breach of contract claim, damages for the notice period
a common law contract claim compensating loss of notice
testPool.modelAnswer: Wrongful dismissal is a common law breach of contract claim. Its damages compensate the financial loss caused by the employer's failure to give proper contractual notice (or an equivalent payment in lieu) — nothing more.

testPool.prompt: Does a wrongful dismissal claim require any minimum length of service?
options: No — it is available from the first day of employment
Yes — the same two-year qualifying period as unfair dismissal

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT something a successful wrongful dismissal claim can recover?
options: Net salary for the unexpired notice period
Contractual benefits that would have accrued during the notice period
Damages for injury to feelings caused by a humiliating dismissal meeting
Accrued but unpaid contractual entitlements due at termination
testPool.trapExplanation: This looks like it should be recoverable because the dismissal genuinely felt humiliating — but Johnson v Unisys forecloses exactly this claim. Injury to feelings and distress caused by the manner of dismissal sit outside the exclusion zone the House of Lords drew around wrongful dismissal damages.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court works through when assessing whether a dismissal was wrongful.
items: Identify the notice period required by the contract (or the s 86 ERA minimum, if higher)
Establish what notice, or payment in lieu, was actually given
Ask whether the shortfall is excused by the employee's own repudiatory breach
If unexcused, calculate damages for the unexpired notice period, subject to mitigation

testPool.prompt: Under s 86 ERA 1996, an employee with nine complete years of continuous service is entitled to how much statutory minimum notice?
options: One week
Nine weeks
Twelve weeks
testPool.explanation: Between two and twelve years' service, the statutory minimum is one week per completed year — nine years means nine weeks. The twelve-week figure is the ceiling reached only at twelve or more years' service.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below summarising Johnson v Unisys, highlight the sentence stating the ratio.
testPool.passage: The claimant argued that the humiliating manner of his dismissal caused him psychiatric injury and should be compensated in contract. The House of Lords held that damages for wrongful dismissal are confined to the financial loss flowing from the employer's failure to give proper notice, and do not extend to injury to feelings, distress or reputational harm caused by the manner of dismissal. Parliament had already created the unfair dismissal scheme to police the fairness and manner of dismissals, with its own remedies and limits.
testPool.ratioSentence: The House of Lords held that damages for wrongful dismissal are confined to the financial loss flowing from the employer's failure to give proper notice, and do not extend to injury to feelings, distress or reputational harm caused by the manner of dismissal.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows the employer has properly exercised a lawful PILON, rather than committed a wrongful dismissal.
testPool.scenarioText: Priya's contract contains an express clause allowing the employer to terminate immediately on payment of salary in lieu of notice. She is called into a meeting, told her employment ends today, and given a final payslip that includes three months' salary and benefits equal to her full notice period.
tappableSpans: express clause allowing the employer to terminate immediately
three months' salary and benefits equal to her full notice period
testPool.correctSpan: express clause allowing the employer to terminate immediately
testPool.explanation: The clause is what makes the whole sequence lawful. Without it, ending the contract today and paying money afterwards would not automatically cure a failure to give notice — the authorisation has to exist in the contract itself.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario gives rise to a wrongful dismissal claim, rather than only a possible unfair dismissal claim?
testPool.scenarioA: An employee with three years' service is dismissed for poor performance after a full, fair capability process, and is given her full six months' contractual notice.
testPool.scenarioB: An employee with three years' service is dismissed for poor performance after a full, fair capability process, but is given no notice and no payment in lieu, despite her contract requiring six months' notice.
testPool.explanation: A involves a procedurally fair dismissal with notice properly given — no breach of contract, so no wrongful dismissal claim (though its fairness could still be tested under the statutory scheme). B breaches the notice term regardless of how fair the underlying reason was — that breach is what wrongful dismissal exists to remedy.

testPool.prompt: An employee dismissed without notice, in breach of a four-month notice clause, finds an equivalent-paying job after one month and works there for the remaining three months. How should her wrongful dismissal damages be assessed?
options: Full four months' pay, with no deduction, because mitigation is irrelevant to wrongful dismissal
One month's pay in full, with the remaining three months reduced to reflect her new earnings under the duty to mitigate
No damages at all, because she found new work
testPool.explanation: The duty to mitigate reduces, rather than extinguishes, the claim: she recovers her loss for the period she was actually out of pocket (the first month) and her damages for the remaining period are offset by what she in fact earned elsewhere.

testPool.prompt: Deniz has a twelve-month notice clause. After a client complaint about his manner (not amounting to gross misconduct), his employer dismisses him on the spot, pays nothing, and tells him to leave the building immediately. Deniz argues the dismissal was also handled in a deliberately humiliating way in front of colleagues, and wants to claim for that distress in addition to his lost notice pay. Analyse his claim.
factsToOrder: Deniz has a twelve-month contractual notice clause
The conduct complained of does not amount to gross misconduct
He is dismissed on the spot with no notice and no payment in lieu
He also seeks damages for the humiliating manner of the dismissal

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Deniz has a wrongful dismissal claim, and whether his damages can include compensation for the manner of the dismissal.
modelAnswer.rule: A dismissal without the contractual notice, and without a lawful PILON, is wrongful unless excused by the employee's own repudiatory breach. Damages are confined to the financial loss caused by the missing notice period; Johnson v Unisys excludes recovery for distress or humiliation caused by how the dismissal was carried out.
modelAnswer.application: The conduct complained of is expressly stated not to amount to gross misconduct, so there is no repudiatory breach by Deniz excusing the employer from giving notice. The failure to give twelve months' notice or an equivalent payment is therefore a straightforward breach. Deniz can recover twelve months' net pay and benefits (subject to mitigation), but his claim for the humiliating manner of the dismissal falls squarely within the Johnson exclusion zone and cannot be added to a wrongful dismissal claim.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Deniz has a wrongful dismissal claim worth up to twelve months' pay and benefits, subject to mitigation; his claim for distress at the manner of dismissal fails as a matter of law.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that garden leave ends the contract of employment immediately?
sliderLabels: Definitely does not end the contract
testPool.explanation: Garden leave keeps the contract alive throughout the notice period — the employee remains paid and bound by contractual duties, just not required to attend work. It is the opposite of a PILON, which is what actually brings the contract to an end early.

testPool.prompt: Why did the stigma damages in Malik survive where the distress damages in Johnson did not?
options: Because Malik was decided by a more senior court
Because Malik's loss arose from the employer's breach of the trust and confidence term during the employment relationship, not from the manner of the dismissal itself
Because Malik's employees had longer service than Mr Johnson
testPool.trapExplanation: Both cases reached the House of Lords, so seniority is not the distinguishing factor, and length of service is irrelevant to either claim. The real distinction is timing and source of the breach: Malik's loss flowed from how the employer ran its business during employment, which is ordinary contractual loss; Johnson's loss flowed from the dismissal event itself, which the House of Lords placed outside the reach of a wrongful dismissal claim.

testPool.prompt: An employee has six years' continuous service and a contract that is silent on notice altogether. What notice is she entitled to?
options: No notice at all, since the contract is silent
The s 86 ERA 1996 statutory minimum for six years' service — six weeks
Twelve weeks, the statutory maximum, applied by default
testPool.explanation: Silence in the contract does not mean no notice — the s 86 ERA statutory minimum applies as a floor regardless of what the contract says, and for six years' service that is six weeks (one week per completed year, between two and twelve years' service).

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is reaching for fairness-based reasoning — was the reason good, was the process fair — when the only question a wrongful dismissal claim asks is whether the contract's notice terms were honoured. A close second is trying to smuggle distress or manner-of-dismissal harm into the damages figure; Johnson v Unisys forecloses that every time.
